title: Yom Kippur: white
hookLine: many wear white, like angels and like burial shrouds
tomorrow: Yom Kippur: the high priest's day

cards: Look around a traditional synagogue on Yom Kippur night and the colors are gone. Men in plain white robes over their clothes, tied with a simple belt. Women in white blouses and dresses.
White covers on the ark and the reading table. Feet in canvas sneakers or socks, because many don't wear leather today. It looks a little like a wedding, and a little like a funeral.

teach.b: The white robe is called a kittel, a Yiddish word for a smock: white cotton or linen, no pockets to speak of, often tied with a white belt.
In many Ashkenazi communities, men wear it on Yom Kippur, and some on Rosh Hashanah too. And it shows up at the big doors of a life.
Many grooms wear a kittel under the wedding canopy. Many leaders of the Passover seder wear one. And many are buried in one, or in plain white shrouds like it.
Why white on Yom Kippur? The great sixteenth-century authority Rabbi Moshe Isserles gives two reasons, and they pull in opposite directions. First, white is the clothing of angels.
On this day, without food or drink, people are said to be like angels, beyond the body's needs, praising all day long.

Second, the kittel is like a burial shroud. Wearing it humbles the heart: it reminds you that life is short and that you'll stand before God with nothing but who you've been. Pure and mortal, angelic and dust, at once.
Behind both is a verse from Isaiah, quoted all through these days: "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow."
Sephardi communities don't usually wear the kittel itself, but many dress in white, and white clothing is a widespread custom, not a rule for everyone. The point isn't fashion.
When everyone wears the same plain white, the rich and the poor look alike. You stand there as a person, nothing more.

how: In many Ashkenazi communities men wear a white kittel on Yom Kippur (and some on Rosh Hashanah); women and Sephardi worshippers often dress in white; many avoid leather shoes on Yom Kippur as one of the day's afflictions.

games.q: you're dressing for Yom Kippur night in a traditional Ashkenazi synagogue. which shoes do many people choose?
o: canvas sneakers or socks, no leather.
games.why: many avoid leather shoes on Yom Kippur, one of the day's traditional afflictions, alongside the white clothing.

practice: If you can, change into something plain, no logos, no jewelry, nothing that tells the world who you are, or just take off one thing, a watch or a ring, and notice what's left when the signals are gone.
If you pray, picture standing before God dressed like everyone else; if not, picture standing in a room where nobody can tell who's important.

wordCard.voice: Kittel. The plain white robe worn on Yom Kippur, at weddings and at the seder, like an angel's garment and like a shroud.
